1.pericope_label: Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature
debates: Whether the cedar is Assyria or Egypt itself
What the waters that made him great stand for
Whether the tree is a cedar or a cypress
outliers: Clarke follows an authority who would render the phrase the tall cedar, so that the whole description belongs to Egypt and Assyria is not in view at all
Gill keeps the Assyrian and rejects the cypress of two ancient versions, since the cypress did not grow in Lebanon
Ellicott holds that Lebanon is named only for its cedars and that Assyria never made it a seat of empire
Keil and Delitzsch explain the comparison as chosen to overthrow all reliance on the might of Egypt
themes: Fruit-bearing trees refusing promotion over the rest
A dominion kept in shape like a tree ordered by a gardener
The utmost security called only the shadow of a tree
Those who excel made the objects of envy

10.pericope_label: I have therefore delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen; he shall surely deal with him: I have driven him out for his wickedness
debates: Who the mighty one of the heathen is
Why a fall already past is spoken of in the future
Whether the birds returning to the fallen trunk are literal or figurative
outliers: Gill canvasses Arbaces, Merodachbaladan and Nebuchadnezzar and prefers the last; Clarke names Nebuchadnezzar, Ellicott his father Nabopolassar, and Wesley Arbaces
Ellicott suggests the future tense is used because the object of the parable is not Assyria but Egypt, whose fall was still to come
Ellicott denies any inconsistency between the nations fleeing at the fall and gathering on the trunk afterwards to fatten on the ruin
Ellicott prefers the marginal stand upon themselves for their height, of princes relying on their own strength
themes: Borrowed feathers fetched back until the tree stood naked
The fallen comforted to see the proud brought as low as themselves
Pride said to have made devils of angels
A covert allusion to the Nile in the constant mention of water

15.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God, in the day when he went down to the grave I caused a mourning
debates: Whether the chapter is about Assyria with Egypt shadowed under it, or about Egypt throughout
What the deep and the floods and the great waters stand for
Who went down to the grave with the fallen king
outliers: Ellicott identifies the deep, the floods and the great waters with the same terms used of the cedar earlier, so that the sources of prosperity are stopped in mourning
Ellicott notes that the word rendered mourn means literally to be black, which suits the figure of Lebanon better than the English
Clarke records an authority who read the whole chapter of the king of Assyria with Egypt only shadowed under it, against his own reading of it as Pharaoh throughout
Wesley reads the comforting of the trees as speech to the dead in the manner of the living, who rejoice to see the proud brought low
themes: A crash heard at a distance across Lebanon
An old tag that the name need only be changed
Subordinate potentates fainting at the fall
